Hon

[2] GEORGE ROBERTSON MP

[3] The British people are rightly proud of their Armed Forces

[4] They want, indeed expect, the Government to provide strong defence

[5] The Strategic Defence Review does just that

[6] Modernising and reshaping our Armed Forces to meet the challenges of the 21st century, this Review will give our Services the firm foundation they need to plan for the long term

[7] The Review is radical, reflecting a changing world, in which the confrontation of the Cold War has been replaced by a complex mixture of uncertainty and instability

[8] These problems pose a real threat to our security, whether in the Balkans, the Middle East or in some troublespot yet to ignite

[9] If we are to discharge our international responsibilities in such areas, we must retain the power to act

[10] Our Armed Forces are Britain's insurance against a huge variety of risks

[11] While the Review will lead to a fundamental reshaping of our forces, I have ensured that it is firmly grounded in foreign policy and sound military experience

[12] It builds on the strengths of our people as well as our long and distinguished military traditions

[13] This mixture of radical change and solid planning has been fused through a process of wide consultation to produce a package which has the wholehearted support of the Service Chiefs of Staff

[14] I too am confident that the Strategic Defence Review will give them the tools to do the job

[15] At the heart of the Review is a series of initiatives across defence to co-ordinate the activities of the three Services more closely, pooling their expertise and maximising their punch, while at the same time eliminating duplication and waste

[16] The most important of these tri-Service "Joint" approaches is the new Joint Rapid Reaction Forces, which will be the spearhead of Britain's modernised, rapidly deployable and better supported front line

[17] As the result of a historic proposal from the First Sea Lord and the Chief of the Air Staff, the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force will build on the success of recent operations in the Gulf and co-operate to develop a new Joint Force

[18] The RAF and RN Harrier jets of this force will be able to operate equally effectively from aircraft carriers or land bases

[19] We will also bring together our battlefield helicopters under a single command, and expand the responsibilities and role of our Chief of Joint Operations

[20] In the post Cold War world, we must be prepared to go to the crisis, rather than have the crisis come to us

[21] So we plan to buy two new larger aircraft carriers to project power more flexibly around the world

[22] New transport aircraft and ships will move our people and equipment rapidly to troublespots

[23] If we ask our forces to fight, we must be sure they will win

[24] That means we must correct the deep-seated problems we inherited from the previous government, most obviously in the medical and logistics areas, to ensure that our forces are properly supported

[25] Past cuts in support have been presented as "trimming the tail without blunting the teeth

[26] The reality is that logistic support is the life-blood of the forces, and we must ensure that our forces get the back up they need

[27] At the same time we must focus our effort on the capabilities we need to be successful today

[28] That will mean reductions in some areas which were needed primarily to meet Cold War threats

[29] So we will place somewhat less emphasis on open ocean anti-submarine warfare and have fewer tanks and fast jets in the front line

[30] We will retain our nuclear deterrent with fewer warheads to meet our twin challenges of minimum credible deterrence backed by a firm commitment to arms control

[31] We will also radically reorganise our procurement and logistics organisations to spur efficiency and drive through best business practice

[32] Then we will use the headroom we have generated to ensure that we have the forces we need to meet the new challenges

[33] Our Reserve Forces must also adapt to the new world

[34] We must make our Reserves relevant and usable by integrating them more closely with regular units and improving their training and specialist skills so that we can deploy them more easily on operations

[35] We should also have a weather eye to the much longer term

[36] Technology is likely to race ahead

[37] It will pose new threats and challenges, such as systematic attacks on computer networks

[38] We must work closely with our Allies to counter these problems

[39] Yet technology may also open up radically new ways for our Armed Forces to operate

[40] Again, we are alive to the possibilities and will work closely with our Allies to ensure that we reap the maximum benefit from such change

[41] This is a massive agenda for change

[42] To design it we have drawn on the skills of all of our people in what I believe is the most open and inclusive defence review ever conducted

[43] Hundreds of experts from within the MOD, the Armed Forces and elsewhere have given a great deal of time over the past year to produce the most significant reshaping of our Armed Forces in a generation

[44] I am very grateful to all of them for the time, energy and ideas they have so generously given

[45] It is absolutely right that we should have consulted so widely; we need to harness the enthusiasm of all of our people to implement these changes and set defence on to a positive road once more

[46] People throughout the Armed Forces have a very large stake in that future, and I have tried to take on as many of their ideas as possible

[47] After a decade of cuts and drift, our people are looking for a positive vision for the future of the Armed Forces, and I believe the Review delivers that

[48] All too often in the past the importance of people in delivering the results we want has been ignored

[49] All three Services have been overstretched because of the demanding pattern of our operations, and I am determined to put that right

[50] We also need to attract and retain the brightest and the best of our young people

[51] To achieve that I intend to expand dramatically the educational opportunities open to members of the Armed Forces, both while they are serving and after they leave the Services

[52] My “Learning Forces” initiative, tied into the Government's “Learning Age” proposals, will give our young people the skills they need to make the best possible contribution to the Armed Forces, and equip them with the transferable qualifications they want once they return to civilian life

[53] We ask our people to do difficult and dangerous jobs, and many of them regularly put their lives on the line

[54] It is therefore right that we should provide them with the best possible equipment

[55] Led by projects such as the world-beating Eurofighter, we will completely overhaul the equipment used by the forces over the next decade

[56] That will be good for our people, and good for Britain's defence industry

[57] To complete this ambitious programme we must apply modern management methods to ensure that we deliver results as efficiently as possible for the taxpayer

[58] Indeed, the continuing push for greater efficiency is an integral part of our plans to drive down costs to pay for the modernisation of our forces

[59] To assist the process we will establish a tri-Service Chief of Defence Logistics, who will be responsible for delivering best business practice throughout our support services

[60] This is another huge change for the Ministry, which will allow us to coordinate and standardise our support services properly for the first time

[61] We are also determined to introduce the best of modern commercial management techniques to the procurement of defence equipment

[62] Too often in the past our new equipment has been too expensive and delivered too late

[63] That is why, as part of the Review, we asked a team from industry, the Services and the consultants McKinsey to study the best ways to learn from companies in areas as diverse as oil exploration and car production, in our search for better ways to provide equipment

[64] Their conclusions will lead to a fundamental overhaul of our procurement processes in my Smart Procurement Initiative

[65] Underpinning the changes to our forces is our reinforced international commitment

[66] NATO will continue as the cornerstone of our defence planning, and we intend to build on our role as a leading European member of the Alliance

[67] Our commitment to the United Nations, through our permanent membership of the Security Council, is also strengthened

[68] We support efforts to help make the UN a more effective tool in resolving international problems

[69] We are also prominent members of the OSCE and the WEU

[70] The British are, by instinct, an internationalist people

[71] We believe that as well as defending our rights, we should discharge our responsiblities in the world

[72] We do not want to stand idly by and watch humanitarian disasters or the aggression of dictators go unchecked

[73] We want to give a lead, we want to be a force for good

[74] That is why the Government is committed to strong defence, and sound defence is sound foreign policy

[75] As Kofi Annan, the UN Secretary General, said "You can do a lot with diplomacy but, of course, you can do a lot more with diplomacy backed up with firmness and force

[76] It is my strong belief that the Strategic Defence Review will deliver Modern Forces for the Modern World which will enable Britain to achieve a lot more in the 21st century

[77] Ministry of Defence July 1998 CHAPTER ONE A STRATEGIC APPROACH TO DEFENCE

[78] The publication of this White Paper fulfils the Government's manifesto commitment to conduct a foreign policy-led strategic defence review to reassess Britain's security interests and defence needs and consider how the roles, missions and capabilities of our Armed Forces should be adjusted to meet the new strategic realities

[79] New Strategic Realities The strategic environment we face today is very different to that of the previous fifty years

[80] The risks and challenges we face are not simply those of the Cold War minus the threat from the Warsaw Pact

[81] It is both better and worse than that

[82] On the positive side, the collapse of Communism and the emergence of democratic states throughout Eastern Europe and in Russia means that there is today no direct military threat to the United Kingdom or Western Europe

[83] Nor do we foresee the re-emergence of such a threat

[84] But we cannot take this for granted

[85] It is therefore a vital British interest that these trends should strengthen and not go into reverse

[86] Our defence policy and activity must contribute to consolidating these welcome changes and thus enhancing our security

[87] The admission of three new democracies to NATO is a major step on this path

[88] But we are determined that this should not lead to new divisions in Europe

[89] NATO's Partnership for Peace and our national programme of bilateral defence co-operation have key roles in promoting and developing constructive security relationships between all the nations of Europe

[90] On the negative side, however, there are new risks to our security and our way of life

[91] During the Cold War, the East/West confrontation dominated strategic thinking in a way that produced a misleading impression of stability in large parts of the world

[92] In part this was because that confrontation temporarily suppressed underlying tensions and problems

[93] In part, it was because the scale of the risks involved in the Cold War obscured the potential importance of the newer style of security risks that were emerging

[94] Instability inside Europe as in Bosnia, and now Kosovo, threatens our security

[95] Instability elsewhere - for example in Africa - may not always appear to threaten us directly

[96] But it can do indirectly, and we cannot stand aside when it leads to massive human suffering

[97] There are still very dangerous regimes in the world

[98] Some are well armed with conventional weapons and their armories assume greater significance as democratic countries reduce their armaments

[99] There is an increasing danger from the proliferation of nuclear, biological and chemical technologies

[100] As Iraq has amply demonstrated, such regimes threaten not only their neighbours but vital economic interests and even international stability

[101] There are also new risks which threaten our security by attacking our way of life

[102] Drugs and organised crime are today powerful enough to threaten the entire fabric of some societies

[103] They certainly pose a serious threat to the well-being of our own society

[104] We have seen new and horrifying forms of terrorism and how serious environmental degradation can cause not only immediate suffering but also dangerous instabilities

[105] And the benefits of the information technology revolution that has swept the world are accompanied by potential new vulnerabilities

[106] The challenge now is to move from stability based on fear to stability based on the active management of these risks, seeking to prevent conflicts rather than suppress them

[107] This requires an integrated external policy through which we can pursue our interests using all the instruments at our disposal, including diplomatic, developmental and military

[108] We must make sure that the Armed Forces can play as full and effective a part in dealing with these new risks as the old

[109] Current Problems It would be as wrong to take military success for granted in this new environment as it would have been during the Cold War

[110] We have therefore taken a hard look at the capabilities of today's Armed Forces

[111] The so-called 'peace dividend' from the ending of the Cold War has already been taken

[112] Since 1990, defence expenditure has fallen by some 23% in real terms and our forces have been cut by nearly a third

[113] Yet over this period we have faced a series of new and largely unexpected operational challenges

[114] Our Armed Forces have responded outstandingly but they face serious problems that carry increasing risks in relation to the changed pattern of operations

[115] There are personnel shortages in important areas, which with the high level of operational commitments are creating excessive and unsustainable pressures on many of our people

[116] Other areas of weakness include the extent of our rapid deployment capabilities and our ability to sustain and support overseas operations, including medical support

[117] Looking Ahead Defence planning is a long term business

[118] Major equipments take years to develop and typically have lives of twenty five years or more

[119] Events since the fall of the Berlin Wall - just nine years ago - show that the political and strategic world can change radically within such timescales

[120] History reminds us that this can be for the worse as well as the better

[121] Social and technological transformation has also been rapid and we can expect this to continue, affecting both our daily lives and the role of our Armed Forces over the next twenty years

[122] We need to take account of such changes and exploit them wherever we can to ensure not only that our forces are as capable and cost-effective as possible but also that they continue to be valued by our society and to provide rewarding careers

[123] The Aim of the Review Defence serves the aims of foreign and security policy

[124] The Government's manifesto sets out a broad vision of Britain's role: strong in defence; resolute in standing up for our own interests and as an advocate of human rights and democracy the world over; a reliable and powerful ally; and a leader in Europe and the international community

[125] Defence can provide a wide range of tools to support these aims

[126] The purpose of the Review was not only to meet the challenges of today's complex international scene but also to provide the flexibility to respond to those we may face well into the new century

[127] We cannot predict the future but if we are to meet it confidently we must have a clear long term view of our objectives and how we expect defence to contribute to them

[128] The Review therefore considers our defence requirements in the period to

[129] We must also show our people that they are getting good value for money for what they spend on defence

[130] For these reasons the Government wishes to achieve a broad national consensus on defence and has consulted widely in the course of the Review

[131] The Strategic Defence Review aims to provide the country with modern, effective and affordable Armed Forces which meet today's challenges but are also flexible enough to adapt to change

[132] It provides a vision for the modernisation of Britain's defence into the 21st century

[133] Its theme is 'Modern Forces for the Modern World

[134] CHAPTER TWO SECURITY PRIORITIES IN A CHANGING WORLD Britain's place in the world is determined by our interests as a nation and as a leading member of the international community

[135] Indeed, the two are inextricably linked because our national interests have a vital international dimension

[136] Interest and Goals We are a major European state and a leading member of the European Union

[137] Our economic and political future is as part of Europe

[138] Our security is indivisible from that of our European partners and allies

[139] We therefore have a fundamental interest in the security and stability of the continent as a whole and in the effectiveness of NATO as a collective political and military instrument to underpin these interests

[140] This in turn depends on the transatlantic relationship and the continued engagement in Europe of the United States

[141] But our vital interests are not confined to Europe

[142] Our economy is founded on international trade

[143] Exports form a higher proportion of Gross Domestic Product than for the US, Japan, Germany or France

[144] We invest more of our income abroad than any other major economy

[145] Our closest economic partners are the European Union and the US but our investment in the developing world amounts to the combined total of France, Germany and Italy

[146] Foreign investment into the UK also provides nearly 20% of manufacturing jobs

[147] We depend on foreign countries for supplies of raw materials, above all oil

[148] Our economic interests and our history give us other international responsibilities

[149] Over million British citizens live and work overseas

[150] We have 13 Overseas Territories spread around the world

[151] We are members of many important international organisations and have developed close ties of friendship with countries in every continent

[152] And as an open society, we are easily affected by global trends and other external influences

[153] Our national security and prosperity thus depend on promoting international stability, freedom and economic development

[154] As a Permanent Member of the UN Security Council and as a country both willing and able to play a leading role internationally we have a responsibility to act as a force for good in the world

[155] We do not aspire to be a world policeman; many of our important national interests and responsibilities are shared with others, particularly our Partners and Allies in the European Union and NATO

[156] We also attach immense importance to the international community as a whole working together through the many multinational organisations, above all the United Nations

[157] THE CHANGING WORLD TO 2015 The post-Cold War environment offers new opportunities to promote these goals and interests but also brings new challenges

[158] And, over the period considered by this Review, there are potential longer term risks to be considered

[159] Over this length of time, there will also be substantial change in the political, social and technological context in which our forces will have to operate

[160] Again, there are opportunities to be exploited and risks to be guarded against

[161] We need to face both with open eyes and recognise that they will bring further changes to our Armed Forces

[162] Opportunities The end of the Cold War has transformed our security environment

[163] The world does not live in the shadow of World War

[164] There is no longer a direct threat to Western Europe or the United Kingdom as we used to know it, and we face no significant military threat to any of our Overseas Territories

[165] The improvement is political as well as military

[166] The end of confrontation has revitalised international bodies and made the 'international community a reality

[167] This is epitomised not only by the role now taken by the UN Security Council but also by the unprecedented international peace support operations in Bosnia which have involved 37 countries operating under a NATO umbrella, including Russia and other members of the former Warsaw Pact

[168] These changes have important implications for the shape of our forces

[169] We do not at present face the threat of an air or other direct attack on this country

[170] Nor do we need large standing forces on the continent or in the Atlantic simply to defend ourselves and our Allies

[171] This has given us the opportunity both to reduce the scale of our forces and to employ them on a wider range of tasks in support of foreign and security policy but this also requires changes in the balance of our military capabilities

[172] The process of restructuring our forces began in the early 1990s but, while the previous government was swift to cut defence expenditure by major cuts in Cold War capabilities, it did not invest adequately in the right capabilities to meet new demands

[173] The first requirement of our foreign and defence policy is to maintain and reinforce the present favourable external security situation

[174] We must consolidate the changes that have taken place in Eastern Europe

[175] Our forces have acquired a new role in promoting our security through programmes designed to promote understanding and trust between all European armed forces and, in particular, to assist the development of modern, democratic forces in Central and Eastern Europe

[176] Such defence diplomacy also has considerable utility in support of wider foreign policy objectives

[177] The next chapter describes the Review's plans for increasing the emphasis we place on this aspect of defence

[178] Current Challenges While we no longer face the threat to our national survival represented by the Warsaw Pact, today's security environment is not benign

[179] This is reflected in the very high level of commitments in which our forces are currently engaged

[180] These arise from a wide range of risks to our security and interests, including combating terrorism related to Northern Ireland

[181] The Government believes that the Belfast Agreement provides the basis for a lasting political settlement

[182] The Armed Forces have already responded flexibly in their deployment following the various ceasefires since

[183] The Government hopes that the level of threat from terrorism will reduce further and allow for reductions in the numbers of troops required to assist the civil authorities consistent with the level of threat, while maintaining normal garrisons as elsewhere in the United Kingdom

[184] While today's commitments are individually on a smaller scale than the Cold War threat, they are operationally demanding, especially in aggregate

[185] At the beginning of the year, we had over 25,000 personnel on operations in Northern Ireland and overseas

[186] This is not unusual

[187] Over the last eight years many more British troops have been on active operations at any one time than during the Cold War

[188] These have ranged from the Gulf War - which was by far our biggest operation since Suez - to the rescue of British citizens from a series of crises overseas

[189] Before considering the implications for our Forces, we need to understand the factors that have contributed to this change

[190] Underlying Risks For the last two hundred years, the dominant force in international affairs has been the nation state

[191] Most wars have been caused by attempts to create or expand such states

[192] In contrast, over the next twenty years, the risks to international stability seem as likely to come from other factors: ethnic and religious conflict; population and environmental pressures; competition for scarce resources; drugs, terrorism and crime

[193] A soldier from The Princess of Wales's Royal Regiment on patrol in West Belfast

[194] These pressures operate both within states and across borders

[195] The break-up of states seems likely to be as much a security problem as traditional expansionism, although Saddam Hussein provides a powerful reminder that this should not be ruled out

[196] Moreover, the consequences of initially local crises may spread dramatically in an ever more interdependent world

[197] Events in Bosnia illustrate this well, with a quarter of a million refugees fleeing to the rest of Europe

[198] Even more worrying was the possibility that the war would ignite tensions over Bosnia's borders, drawing in other states

[199] Overspill of this kind could lead to pressures which might weaken or undermine some of the new democracies in the region and even put at risk wider European security

[200] Events in Kosovo emphasise the continuing dangers and the need to be able to mount a military response rapidly to contain crises before they get out of hand

[201] Impact of Social and Technological Change Social and technological change are already having a huge impact both on the nature of the risks we face and our options for responding to them

[202] Indeed, technology is a major force in social change worldwide

[203] We can expect such change to continue and probably accelerate

[204] In military capability, we can look, for example, for much more precise application of force as a result of improvements in intelligence gathering, command and control and precision weapons

[205] Equally, there is potential for practical and cost benefits in the way we train and support our forces

[206] Such possibilities also raise difficult long term questions

[207] How much should we invest in improving "enabling technologies" at the expense of weapon numbers

[208] How can our equipment plans keep up with the pace of change

[209] How do we and our Allies retain interoperability with US forces given the radical changes they envisage

[210] And will technological changes also require radical changes in the way our forces are organised and fight

[211] We will be addressing these issues in the coming years

[212] Technological and social change will also open up broader possibilities which will have a profound effect on our future security

[213] Many of these developments will be double-edged, bringing new vulnerabilities as well as opportunities

[214] They include new ways of fighting such as information warfare (which attacks through the computer systems on which both our forces and civil society increasingly depend); greater pressures on operational decisions (instant media reporting from both sides of the front line); the wider spread of technologies which may be used against us (such as biological weapons); and highly sophisticated civil capabilities that will be readily available both for us and potential adversaries. They include new ways of fighting such as information warfare (which attacks through the computer systems on which both our forces and civil society increasingly depend); greater pressures on operational decisions (instant media reporting from both sides of the front line); the wider spread of technologies which may be used against us (such as biological weapons); and highly sophisticated civil capabilities that will be readily available both for us and potential adversaries. strategies

[215] And where we (and our Allies) exploit technology to strengthen our existing superiority in conventional weapons, our potential adversaries may choose to adopt alternative weapons and unconventional (or 'asymmetric') strategies, perhaps attacking us through vulnerabilities in our open civil societies

[216] While we cannot predict the detailed impact of such changes over twenty years, we have taken a hard look at how we can seek to make the most of emerging trends in all areas of the Review, including how to adapt our requirements and procurement processes so that we are not left behind by the speed of change

[217] SECURITY PRIORITIES FOR THE FUTURE European Security European security will remain fundamental to our national security and economic well-being

[218] We must not take that security for granted

[219] We need to work to preserve it, through strengthening international security relationships and responding to new risks of instability within Europe, as in Bosnia

[220] We also need to preserve our capability to react should the political climate change for the worse

[221] Membership of NATO will continue to provide the UK with its best insurance against all these risks

[222] This partnership between Europe and North America has been a uniquely effective political and military security Alliance for half a century

[223] The fundamental purpose of defending the freedom of all its members remains as important as ever

[224] NATO has also shown it is highly relevant to the specific circumstances of Europe today

[225] Militarily, NATO has been reinvigorated and has shown its continuing value by its role in Bosnia and its response to events in Kosovo

[226] Politically, it has responded positively and imaginatively to the aspirations of the new European democracies

[227] The planned admission in 1999 of three new members from the former Warsaw Pact is a welcome first step in a carefully managed process of enlargement which will strengthen both the Alliance itself and European security as a whole

[228] NATO's Partnership for Peace programme and its Agreements with Russia and the Ukraine are also part of this positive approach to strengthening political and security relationships in Europe

[229] The Queen's Royal Hussars on patrol in a Challenger 1 main battle tank in Bosnia

[230] A wide range of other institutions also have major parts to play in the development and reinforcement of European security

[231] The European Union has a vital role in helping to preserve and extend economic prosperity and political stability, including through the Common Foreign and Security Policy

[232] The Western European Union has an important role in fostering defence co-operation amongst its members, in conflict prevention and, particularly, peacekeeping

[233] Development of the European Security and Defence Identity within NATO will enable the Western European Union to carry out these roles more effectively

[234] And the Government places high importance on the role of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe which embraces 54 states and is uniquely placed to contribute to building confidence and preventing conflict in Europe

[235] Outside Europe Outside Europe our interests are most likely to be affected by events in the Gulf and the Mediterranean

[236] Instability in these areas also carries wider risks

[237] We have particularly important national interests and close friendships in the Gulf

[238] Oil supplies from the Gulf are crucial to the world economy

[239] Confrontation in the Middle East carries the risk of escalation and since the region borders on NATO, in some circumstances crises could involve the Alliance directly

[240] The same is true, to a lesser extent, in North Africa

[241] Although our direct interests in the region are limited, its proximity to the southern boundary of the European Union and NATO gives us a continuing stake in its stability

[242] There are already significant sources of instability in these regions - including the continuing threat represented by Saddam Hussein's Iraq

[243] The presence and potential spread of ballistic missiles, chemical and biological weapons and even nuclear weapons add to the risks

[244] These dangers seem unlikely to diminish and may grow

[245] Many of our Allies and Partners have similar important interests and friendships in these areas

[246] We would therefore expect to work with them in responding to any future crises

[247] Elsewhere, although the risks to our specific interests are small, we have longstanding international friendships to maintain and we have an important wider interest in supporting international order and in promoting freedom, democracy and prosperity

[248] Our international stature and position as a Permanent Member of the UN Security Council gives us a particular responsibility to contribute

[249] Nor does the British public expect us to turn our back on poverty, inequality and human suffering in poorer countries

[250] We will respond to such problems as necessary drawing on the range of civil, diplomatic, economic and military means at our disposal

[251] Soldiers of The Princess of Wales's Royal Regiment make friends with children in Brazzaville whilst on standby with RAF Puma helicopters to evacuate British civilians from Zaire

[252] This chapter has considered Britain's security priorities in a changing world

[253] Pursuing these priorities requires the combined application of all the means at our disposal

[254] Military action is one of those means but will seldom be sufficient on its own

[255] We require armed forces which can operate in support of diplomacy alongside economic, trade and developmental levers, to strengthen security and avert conflict as well as conducting effective military operations if required

[256] Starting from these security priorities, the Review re-examined the broad Missions and more specific military tasks for our forces to form a basis for planning, taking into account their contribution to other policy objectives

[257] The revised Missions cover both current priorities and longer term insurance: (a) Peacetime Security (b) Security of the Overseas Territories (c) Defence Diplomacy (d) Support to Wider British Interests (e) Peace Support and Humanitarian Operations (f) Regional Conflict outside the NATO area (g) Regional Conflict inside the NATO area (h) Strategic Attack on NATO

[258] The new Missions The broad scope of defence activity covered by these Missions is similar to recent years but there are significant changes in the balance between the Missions and in the specific military tasks that underpin them

[259] Defence Diplomacy becomes a Mission in its own right, reflecting the importance to our security of building and maintaining trust and preventing conflict, particularly in Europe

[260] We anticipate continuing and perhaps growing calls for contributions to international peace support and humanitarian operations, some of which could be militarily very demanding

[261] For the foreseeable future, we envisage that the largest operation we might have to undertake would be involvement in a major regional conflict, whether as part of NATO or a wider international coalition

[262] We need, however, to retain a basis on which we could reconstitute larger capabilities should a strategic threat to NATO ever begin to re-emerge

[263] A submarine simulator at HMS NEPTUNE's Submarine Command Team Training School

[264] Support against terrorism of all kinds will remain of the highest priority for the foreseeable future

[265] As in the last few years, our forces may be called on more frequently to assist, often in co-operation with other nations, with the evacuation of British (and other) citizens caught up in overseas crises

[266] There may well be an increased requirement for some specialist support to civil authorities, for example in countering drug related crime. Overseas Territories

[267] The security of our Overseas Territories is a fundamental government responsibility

[268] Although there are at present no significant military threats to these territories, our forces must be able to react to any emerging security problem, including from drugs and international crime, and where necessary to assist the civil authorities

[269] We will, therefore, continue to provide garrisons and other forms of military presence as appropriate, including in the Falklands, Cyprus, Gibraltar and the Caribbean, and maintain the capability to supplement these as needed

[270] The Armed Forces and the Ministry of Defence have considerable experience and expertise in conflict prevention work but the creation of a formal Defence Diplomacy Mission will make this a core defence activity

[271] This will give it greater priority and ensure that it is properly linked to the Government's broader policy objectives

[272] Troops from Poland and Ukraine train in the UK with the 2nd Battalion The Parachute Regiment on Exercise Cossack Steppe

[273] The new Mission covers arms control, non-proliferation and related security building measures; our Outreach programme in Eastern Europe; and wider military assistance and training for overseas countries

[274] We intend to improve the effectiveness of our existing activities and increase our effort in all these areas including: – an enhanced arms control programme incorporating an improved 'Open Skies' capability to monitor arms control agreements and additional training in arms control inspection techniques; – an expansion of the Outreach programme including greater use of attachments and short term training teams, and additional training courses

[275] A particular aspect of this programme is explaining the importance of accountability, and the role and value of civilians in defence management; – wider education and training initiatives, to help develop the skills and structures needed by modern democratically accountable forces

[276] This will include the establishment of a Defence Diplomacy scholarship scheme at the Joint Services Command and Staff College and providing extra manpower for short term in-country tasks

[277] We are also undertaking a worldwide reassessment of our requirement for defence attachés in the new international environment, taking particular account of their key part in defence diplomacy

[278] We expect to create a number of new posts, including some specifically to support the expanded Outreach programme, and selection, training and career management of attachés will place increased emphasis on the qualities and skills needed for this role

[279] Wider British Interests

[280] We see no diminution in the value of the activities which our forces undertake in support of British interests and standing overseas

[281] They will continue to have a particular role in demonstrating our commitment to our international friendships worldwide, for example through our contribution to the Five Power Defence Arrangements in South East Asia

[282] There are many ways in which they can assist broader national objectives and interests, including valuable training and support for British exports

[283] Peace Support and Humanitarian Operations

[284] In a less stable world, we have seen more international operations of this type

[285] The trends identified earlier suggest that this will continue

[286] Britain will play its full part in such international efforts

[287] At one end of the spectrum, this might involve logistic or medical support to a disaster relief operation

[288] At the other, it might involve major combat operations as we were prepared to undertake when NATO's Intervention Force (IFOR) first deployed to Bosnia

[289] Our forces have developed particular experience and expertise in operations of this kind

[290] We regard it as important to strengthen the effectiveness of the international community in peace support and humanitarian operations of all kinds and in co-ordinating between political, humanitarian and military operations

[291] But we attach particular priority to enhancing the abilities of the UN in this area

[292] Many of the improvements in capability set out in Chapter 5 will have a direct application in peace support and humanitarian deployments

[293] As a Permanent Member of the Security Council, we intend to give a lead by making our national contribution to UN operations more effective

[294] We will also make a much larger proportion of our front line capabilities potentially available to the UN for such contingencies, including all of our rapidly deployable forces

[295] And our new Joint Defence Centre (see Chapter 9) will have a particular responsibility for contributing to the development of international peace support doctrine

[296] Regional Conflict Outside NATO

[297] Outside Europe, the greatest risks to our national economic and political interests - and probably to international stability - will remain in the Gulf

[298] Regional conflict in North Africa or the Near East could, in some circumstances, also affect our interests and those of our Allies

[299] As the 1990/91 Gulf War and subsequent events have shown, this Mission may involve major combat operations as well as early, deterrent deployments

[300] Such operations also impose demanding requirements, for example, in relation to strategic transport for deployment and supply, and to command and control

[301] NATO Regional Conflict

[302] Britain has always made a major political and military contribution to NATO's capability for collective defence

[303] This will continue to be at the heart of our defence policy

[304] NATO now longer faces a Cold War threat but circumstances could arise in which Alliance members were threatened by a smaller scale but still militarily demanding regional crisis or conflict

[305] NATO must therefore continue to provide a military capability to deter and if necessary respond to such crises

[306] This includes the maintenance of a capability to deter the threat or use of nuclear weapons

[307] The full range of Britain's military capabilities will continue to be available to NATO; in particular, we shall maintain our leading role in its Rapid Reaction Corps

[308] Strategic Attack on NATO

[309] No threat on this scale is in prospect

[310] It would, however, be unwise to conclude that one could never reappear but the conventional forces needed to threaten such an attack would take many years to create

[311] This Mission therefore provides for longer-term insurance through a credible nuclear deterrent and the retention of the essential military capabilities on which we could rebuild larger forces over a long period, if circumstances were radically to worsen

[312] The pattern of demands on our forces which emerges is very different from that of the Cold War

[313] In operational terms, the most demanding individual scenario against which we must now plan is no longer all-out war in Europe but a major regional crisis involving our national interest, perhaps on NATO's periphery or in the Gulf

[314] Apart from scale, however, the new international environment is in many ways more demanding

[315] Undertaking smaller but frequent, often simultaneous and sometimes prolonged operations can be more difficult than preparing for a single worst-case conflict

[316] During the 1990s, we have deployed or been prepared to deploy forces on a wide range of operations at various levels, in addition to maintaining our day-to-day responsibilities

[317] Against the security priorities described earlier we can expect this trend to continue

[318] There is a new emphasis on defence diplomacy and on the use of armed forces to support diplomacy in efforts to deter or manage crises, from humanitarian missions to UN embargoes and peacekeeping

[319] Crises often occur with little warning and we need to be able to respond rapidly

[320] In order to deter, and where deterrence fails, we must maintain forces which can be successful in conventional warfighting

[321] Indeed most of the military capabilities required are equally valuable in support of the wider range of tasks we now face

[322] All this places a premium on the flexibility and usability of the Armed Forces in the modern world

[323] We could of course, as a country, choose to take a narrow view of our role and responsibilities which did not require a significant military capability

[324] This would mean that we would not wish and would not be able to contribute effectively to resolving crises such as Bosnia, Kosovo, or the invasion of Kuwait

[325] This is indeed a real choice, but not one the Government could recommend for Britain

[326] CHAPTER FOUR DETERRENCE AND DISARMAMENT Deterrence is about preventing war rather than fighting it

[327] All our forces have an important deterrent role but nuclear deterrence raises particularly difficult issues because of the nature of nuclear war

[328] The Government wishes to see a safer world in which there is no place for nuclear weapons

[329] Progress on arms control is therefore an important objective of foreign and defence policy

[330] Nevertheless, while large nuclear arsenals and risks of proliferation remain, our minimum deterrent remains a necessary element of our security

[331] The Strategic Defence Review has conducted a rigorous re-examination of our deterrence requirements

[332] This does not depend on the size of other nation's arsenals but on the minimum necessary to deter any threat to our vital interests

[333] We have concluded that we can safely make further significant reductions from Cold War levels, both in the number of weapons and in our day-to-day operating posture

[334] Transparency about nuclear weapons holdings also plays a part in arms control and, although we cannot give precise details of all aspects of our deterrent, we intend to be significantly more open in some areas

[335] With the withdrawal of the last RAF WE177 bombs in March 1998, Trident is our only nuclear weapon

[336] We need to ensure that it can remain an effective deterrent for up to 30 years

[337] This is why we need a force of four Trident submarines

[338] The last of these, Vengeance, will be launched later this year

[339] Trident submarine, HMS VICTORIOUS, on trials

[340] Similarly, we must judge our weapons requirements against the worst circumstances that we might face over Trident's life, however remote they may seem today

[341] The credibility of deterrence also depends on retaining an option for a limited strike that would not automatically lead to a full scale nuclear exchange

[342] Unlike Polaris and Chevaline, Trident must also be capable of performing this 'sub-strategic' role

[343] Against this background, taking into account Trident's greater accuracy than Polaris, the Review has concluded that we need a stockpile of less than 200 operationally available warheads

[344] This is a reduction of a third from the maximum of 300 announced by the previous government and represents a reduction of more than 70% in the potential explosive power of the deterrent since the end of the Cold War
